head: Number
Breaks into

tips: A number divides by every combination of its prime factors: \(12=2\cdot2\cdot3\), therefore \(2\), \(3\), \(4\), \(6\) and \(12\) divide it.
To test a divisor, check its prime ingredients — unpack non-prime bases like \(6\) or \(10^2\) first.
Quick test for \(3\): add the digits. \(87\): \(8+7=15\), and \(15\) divides by \(3\), therefore \(87\) does too.

steps.stem: \(x\) and \(y\) are integers that are not prime, and \(x<20<y\). Between \(x\) and \(20\) there are exactly \(2\) prime numbers (not including \(x\)). Between \(20\) and \(y\) there are exactly \(2\) prime numbers (not including \(y\)). What is the smallest possible value of \(x\cdot y\)?
explanation: Below \(20\): the two primes must be \(17\) and \(19\), and \(13\) must stay out. Therefore \(13\le x<17\). \(x\) is not prime, therefore \(x\) is \(14\), \(15\) or \(16\).
Above \(20\): the two primes must be \(23\) and \(29\), and \(31\) must stay out. Therefore \(29<y\le31\). \(y=31\) is prime (not allowed), therefore \(y=30\).
The smallest product: \(14\cdot30=420\).

steps.stem: Given: \(x\) is a prime number, and \(x^5\) is a two-digit number. \(7x=?\)
explanation: Test the smallest primes.
\(x=3\): \(3^5=243\), three digits ✗. Bigger primes give even bigger fifth powers.

steps.stem: Given: \(x=3\cdot2^3\cdot10^2\). Which of the following numbers does not divide \(x\)?
explanation: Break the non-prime factor into primes: \(10^2=(2\cdot5)^2=2^2\cdot5^2\). Therefore \(x=2^5\cdot3\cdot5^2\).
Check each choice: \(15=3\cdot5\) ✓, \(20=2^2\cdot5\) ✓, \(30=2\cdot3\cdot5\) ✓.
\(21=3\cdot7\), and \(x\) has no \(7\). So \(21\) does not divide \(x\).

steps.stem: Which of the following numbers is prime?
explanation: Test each number with the primes up to its square root.
\(91=7\cdot13\), \(119=7\cdot17\) and \(133=7\cdot19\). None of them is prime.
\(113\) is odd. Its digit sum is \(1+1+3=5\), therefore \(3\) does not divide it. It does not end in \(0\) or \(5\). \(113=7\cdot16+1\), therefore \(7\) does not divide it.
No prime up to \(\sqrt{113}\) divides it, therefore \(113\) is prime.

steps.title: Factor tools — review card
steps.intro: The two "greatest divisor" wordings, their official names, and the divisor facts.

head: Question says
Do this
Example
rows: Greatest COMMON divisor (GCD) of two numbers
Primes in both, each at its LOWER power
Greatest GUARANTEED divisor (divides by both) = least common multiple (LCM)
Every prime, each at its HIGHER power
GCD × LCM = the two numbers multiplied

tips: Divides by \(2\) and \(5\) → by \(10\). Divides by \(2\) and \(6\) → only \(6\) is sure (the \(2\) is inside the \(6\)).
Trap: multiplying the two numbers. \(8\cdot12=96\), but the LCM of \(8\) and \(12\) is \(24\), because they share the prime \(2\).
Letters as primes? Plug in the smallest primes \(2\), \(3\), \(5\), \(7\) in the right order, then check every choice.

steps.stem:
\(a\), \(b\), \(c\), \(d\) are different prime numbers.
Given:
\(\begin{cases} x=a^2\cdot b\cdot c^4\cdot d \\ y=a^3\cdot c^2\cdot d^2 \end{cases}\)
What is the greatest common divisor (GCD) of \(x\) and \(y\)?
explanation: GCD: take each prime that is in both numbers, at its LOWER power.
\(b\) is only in \(x\), therefore it is not in the GCD.
GCD \(=a^2\cdot c^2\cdot d\). (Choice (3) takes the higher powers: that is the LCM.)

steps.stem: A number is divisible without remainder by both \(8\) and \(12\). What is the greatest number that is guaranteed to divide it?
explanation: Break into primes: \(8=2^3\) and \(12=2^2\cdot3\).
The number divides by both, therefore it divides by their least common multiple (LCM): every prime at its HIGHER power. \(2^3\cdot3=24\).
Nothing bigger is guaranteed: the number could be \(24\) itself, and \(48\) does not divide \(24\).
The trap: \(8\cdot12=96\). The two numbers share the prime \(2\), therefore their product is too big.

steps.stem: \(x\) is a three-digit number made only of the digits \(1\), \(2\) and \(3\) (a digit may repeat). Which of the following cannot be the product of the digits of \(x\)?
explanation: Each digit is \(1\), \(2\) or \(3\), therefore the product is built only from the primes \(2\) and \(3\).
\(10=2\cdot5\) needs the prime \(5\), and no digit gives it. So \(10\) is impossible.

steps.stem:
\(x\) and \(y\) are positive integers, and neither of them is \(1\).
Given:
\(\begin{cases} x\cdot y=36 \\ A=|x-y| \end{cases}\)
What is the difference between the greatest possible value of \(A\) and the smallest possible value of \(A\)?
explanation: Break \(36\) into pairs of factors (without \(1\)): \(2\cdot18\), \(3\cdot12\), \(4\cdot9\), \(6\cdot6\).
Greatest \(A=16\), smallest \(A=0\). The difference: \(16-0=16\).

steps.stem: You multiply two or more of the numbers \(2\), \(3\) and \(7\) (each number at most once). What is the sum of all the different products you can get?
explanation: Products of two numbers: \(2\cdot3=6\), \(2\cdot7=14\), \(3\cdot7=21\).
Product of all three: \(2\cdot3\cdot7=42\).
Sum: \(6+14+21+42=83\). (Forgetting \(42\) gives \(41\) — the trap.)

steps.stem: Given: \(y^2\) is a prime number. Which of the following is necessarily true?
explanation: If \(y\) were an integer with \(|y|>1\), then \(y^2=y\cdot y\) would break into two factors bigger than \(1\). It would not be prime.
If \(y\) were \(0\), \(1\) or \(-1\), then \(y^2\) would be \(0\) or \(1\). These are not prime either.
So \(y\) is not an integer. Example: \(y=\sqrt3\) gives \(y^2=3\), a prime.

steps.stem:
\(n\) is a positive integer with exactly \(3\) different divisors (including \(1\) and \(n\)).
Given: \(B=\sqrt{n}\).
How many divisors does \(B\) have (including \(1\) and \(B\))?
explanation: Exactly \(3\) divisors means \(n=p^2\) for a prime \(p\). Its divisors are \(1\), \(p\) and \(p^2\).
\(B=\sqrt{p^2}=p\), a prime.
A prime has exactly \(2\) divisors: \(1\) and itself. Example: \(n=49\), \(B=7\), and the divisors of \(7\) are \(1\) and \(7\).

steps.title: More factor tools
steps.intro: Three tools. Each one starts with breaking the number into primes.

head: Tool
Rule
Example
rows: break into primes, then match the exponents
it divides one of the factors

tips: Only for primes: \(6\) divides \(4\cdot9=36\), but \(6\) divides neither \(4\) nor \(9\).
In "not necessarily true" questions, a statement that is never true is also not necessarily true.

steps.stem:
\(a\) and \(b\) are positive integers.
Given: \(2^a\cdot3^b=108\).
\(a-b=?\)
explanation: Break \(108\) into primes: \(108=4\cdot27=2^2\cdot3^3\).
A number breaks into primes in only one way, therefore match the exponents: \(2^a\cdot3^b=2^2\cdot3^3\) gives \(a=2\) and \(b=3\).
\(a-b=2-3=-1\). (Swapping \(a\) and \(b\) gives \(1\) — the trap.)

steps.stem: \(a\) and \(b\) are prime numbers. Which of the following numbers cannot be \(a+b\)?
explanation: All four choices are odd. An odd sum of two primes needs one even prime, and the only even prime is \(2\).
So check whether the choice minus \(2\) is prime.
\(27=2+25\), and \(25=5^2\) is not prime ✗. So the sum cannot be \(27\).

steps.stem:
\(a\) and \(b\) are prime numbers.
Exactly two of the numbers \(10\), \(15\), \(7\) are divisible by \(a\).
Exactly one of the numbers \(22\), \(15\), \(30\) is divisible by \(b\).
\(a\cdot b=?\)
explanation: Break into primes: \(10=2\cdot5\), \(15=3\cdot5\), \(7=7\). Only the prime \(5\) is in exactly two of them. So \(a=5\).
\(22=2\cdot11\), \(15=3\cdot5\), \(30=2\cdot3\cdot5\). The primes \(2\), \(3\) and \(5\) are each in two of them. Only \(11\) is in exactly one. So \(b=11\).
\(a\cdot b=5\cdot11=55\).

steps.stem:
\(a\) and \(b\) are positive integers.
Given:
\(\begin{cases} a<b \\ a\cdot b+2a=36 \end{cases}\)
Which of the following cannot be the value of \(a+b\)?
explanation: Take out the common factor \(a\): \(a(b+2)=36\).
\(a=6\): \(b+2=6\), \(b=4<a\) ✗. A bigger \(a\) gives an even smaller \(b\) ✗.
The possible sums are \(35\), \(18\), \(13\) and \(11\). \(15\) is not possible.

steps.stem:
\(a\), \(b\), \(c\), \(d\) are prime numbers, and \(a<b<c<d\).
Given: \(y=a^d\cdot b^c\).
Which of the following necessarily divides \(y\)?
explanation: \(y\) is built from the prime \(a\) (\(d\) times) and the prime \(b\) (\(c\) times).
\(a^c\): \(c<d\), therefore \(y\) has enough \(a\)s ✓. \(b^a\): \(a<c\), therefore \(y\) has enough \(b\)s ✓. So \(a^c\cdot b^a\) divides \(y\).
\(b^d\): \(y\) has only \(c\) copies of \(b\), and \(c<d\) ✗. \(c\) and \(d^b\): the primes \(c\) and \(d\) are not factors of \(y\) at all ✗.
With the smallest primes: \(a=2\), \(b=3\), \(c=5\), \(d=7\) give \(y=2^7\cdot3^5\), and of the four choices only \(2^5\cdot3^2\) divides it.

steps.stem:
\(a\), \(b\), \(c\) are different positive integers.
Given: \(x=a\cdot b\cdot c\) is divisible by \(15\) without remainder.
Which of the following statements is not necessarily true?
choices: At least one of \(a\), \(b\), \(c\) is divisible by \(5\).
It is possible that exactly one of \(a\), \(b\), \(c\) is divisible by \(15\).
If \(a\) and \(b\) are not divisible by \(3\), then \(c^2\) is divisible by \(9\).
The number of different prime divisors of \(x^2\) is greater than that of \(x\).
explanation: (1) Always true: \(5\) is prime and divides \(a\cdot b\cdot c\), therefore it divides one of the factors.
(3) Always true: \(3\) is prime and divides \(a\cdot b\cdot c\). It does not divide \(a\) or \(b\), therefore it divides \(c\). Then \(c^2\) is divisible by \(3^2=9\).
(4) Never true: squaring doubles the exponents but adds no new prime. For example, \(15=3\cdot5\) and \(225=3^2\cdot5^2\) have the same two primes.
Never true is also "not necessarily true", therefore the answer is (4).

steps.stem:
\(a\) and \(b\) are positive integers. \(a\) has exactly two prime factors: \(2\) and \(5\). \(b\) has exactly two prime factors: \(2\) and \(7\).
Given: \(b<a\).
What is the smallest possible value of \(\frac{a\cdot b}{35}\)?
explanation: Numbers with exactly the prime factors \(2\) and \(5\): \(10\), \(20\), \(40\), \(50\), … Numbers with exactly the prime factors \(2\) and \(7\): \(14\), \(28\), \(56\), …
The expression is smallest when \(a\) and \(b\) are smallest. The smallest \(b\) is \(14\). Since \(b<a\), \(a=10\) is too small. The smallest \(a\) is \(20\).

steps.stem:
\(a\) is an integer.
Given: \(1<a<150\), and \(a\) has exactly \(3\) different divisors (including \(1\) and \(a\)).
How many different values can \(a\) have?
explanation: A number with exactly \(3\) divisors is a prime squared: its divisors are \(1\), \(p\) and \(p^2\).
So there are \(5\) values.

steps.stem: Which of the following numbers is prime?
explanation: \(29\): \(\sqrt{29}<6\), therefore try \(2\), \(3\), \(5\). None of them divides \(29\), therefore \(29\) is prime.

steps.stem: How many positive divisors does \(2^3\cdot3^2\) have?
explanation: Each exponent plus \(1\), multiplied: \((3+1)(2+1)=4\cdot3=12\).

steps.stem: What is the greatest common divisor (GCD) of \(36\) and \(54\)?
explanation: GCD: each shared prime at its lower power: \(2\cdot3^2=18\).

steps.stem: What is the least common multiple (LCM) of \(12\) and \(18\)?
explanation: LCM: every prime at its higher power: \(2^2\cdot3^2=36\).
Check: \(36=3\cdot12=2\cdot18\) ✓. (\(72\) is a common multiple too, but not the least one.)

steps.stem: \(p\) and \(q\) are prime numbers, and \(p\cdot q=91\). \(p+q=?\)
explanation: \(91\) looks prime, but it is not: \(\sqrt{91}<10\), and \(91=7\cdot13\).
So the primes are \(7\) and \(13\), and \(7+13=20\).

steps.stem: \(a\) and \(b\) are prime numbers smaller than \(20\), and \(b<a\). What is the greatest possible value of \(a-b\)?
explanation: Take the greatest prime below \(20\) and the smallest prime: \(a=19\) and \(b=2\).

steps.stem: What is the sum of the greatest one-digit prime number and the greatest two-digit prime number?
explanation: The greatest one-digit prime is \(7\) (\(8\) and \(9\) are not prime).
The greatest two-digit prime is \(97\) (\(98\) is even and \(99=9\cdot11\)).

steps.stem: Given: \(x=2^2\cdot5^3\). Which of the following numbers divides \(x\) without remainder?
What is the smallest positive integer \(k\) such that \(18k\) is a perfect square?
explanation: \(18=2\cdot3^2\). In a perfect square every exponent is even.
The \(2\) has exponent \(1\), therefore it needs one more \(2\): \(k=2\).

steps.stem: A calculator shows the number \(1\). Only two keys work: "\(\times2\)" and "\(\times7\)". You may press them as many times as you like. Which of the following numbers can you not reach?
explanation: Every number you can reach is built only from the primes \(2\) and \(7\).
\(42=2\cdot3\cdot7\) needs the prime \(3\) ✗. So \(42\) cannot be reached.

steps.stem: How many prime numbers are there between \(80\) and \(100\)?
explanation: Even numbers and numbers ending in \(5\) are not prime. That leaves \(81\), \(83\), \(87\), \(89\), \(91\), \(93\), \(97\), \(99\).
\(83\), \(89\) and \(97\): the root is less than \(10\), and \(2\), \(3\), \(5\), \(7\) do not divide them. They are prime.
So there are \(3\) primes.

steps.stem: What is the sum of all the prime numbers between \(50\) and \(60\)?
explanation: The odd numbers between \(50\) and \(60\) that do not end in \(5\): \(51\), \(53\), \(57\), \(59\).
\(53\) and \(59\): the root is less than \(8\), and \(2\), \(3\), \(5\), \(7\) do not divide them. They are prime.

steps.stem:
\(a\) is an odd one-digit prime, and \(b\) is a two-digit prime smaller than \(30\).
Given: \(x=a\cdot b\).
Which of the following gives the most precise range for \(x\)?
explanation: Smallest \(x=3\cdot11=33\). Greatest \(x=7\cdot29=203\).

steps.stem: A number is called "interesting" if the sum of all the prime numbers from \(2\) up to that number (including it) is a prime number. Which of the following numbers is "interesting"?
explanation: Only \(4\) is "interesting".

steps.stem: Dana wrote a poem of \(5\) lines. The first line has \(20\) words. Each of the other lines has the smallest prime number of words that is greater than the number of words in the line before it. How many words are in the last line?
explanation: Line 1 has \(20\) words. Line 2: the next prime after \(20\) is \(23\) (\(21=3\cdot7\), and \(22\) is even).
Line 3: \(29\) (\(25\) and \(27\) are not prime). Line 4: \(31\).

steps.stem: Which of the following numbers has the greatest number of different divisors?
explanation: \(13\) is prime: \(2\) divisors.
\(55=5\cdot11\): \(2\cdot2=4\) divisors. \(87=3\cdot29\) (a fake prime: \(8+7=15\) divides by \(3\)): \(4\) divisors.
The answer is \(66\).

steps.stem: Given: \(p\) is an odd prime. What is the greatest common divisor of \(p\) and \(2p+1\)?
explanation: The only divisors of the prime \(p\) are \(1\) and \(p\).
\(2p+1\) divided by \(p\) leaves a remainder of \(1\), therefore \(p\) does not divide \(2p+1\).
So the GCD is \(1\). Check with \(p=3\): the GCD of \(3\) and \(7\) is \(1\) ✓.

steps.stem: \(p\) and \(q\) are different prime numbers. Which of the following cannot be the difference between them?
explanation: All four choices are odd. An odd difference of two primes needs one even prime: \(2\). So the bigger prime is the choice plus \(2\).
\(23+2=25=5^2\) is not prime ✗. So the difference cannot be \(23\).

steps.stem:
\(p\), \(q\), \(r\) are different prime numbers.
Given:
\(\begin{cases} M=p^2\cdot q^3\cdot r \\ N=p^3\cdot q\cdot r^2 \end{cases}\)
What is the greatest common divisor (GCD) of \(M\) and \(N\)?
explanation: GCD: take each prime that is in both numbers, at its LOWER power.
GCD \(=p^2\cdot q\cdot r\). (Choice 3 takes the higher powers: that is the LCM.)

steps.stem:
\(p\) and \(q\) are different prime numbers.
Given:
\(\begin{cases} M=p^3\cdot q \\ N=p^2\cdot q^4 \end{cases}\)
What is the least common multiple (LCM) of \(M\) and \(N\)?
explanation: LCM: every prime at its higher power.
LCM \(=p^3\cdot q^4\). (\(p^2\cdot q\) is the GCD, and \(p^5\cdot q^5=M\cdot N\) is too big.)

steps.stem:
\(p\) and \(q\) are prime numbers.
Given: \(p^2\cdot q=75\).
\(p+q=?\)
explanation: Break \(75\) into primes: \(75=3\cdot25=3\cdot5^2\).
The prime that is squared is \(5\), therefore \(p=5\) and \(q=3\).

steps.stem: \(k\) is a positive integer, and \(2^3\cdot3^4\cdot5\cdot k\) is a perfect square. What is the smallest possible value of \(k\)?
explanation: In a perfect square every exponent is even.
\(2^3\): odd exponent, needs one more \(2\). \(3^4\): even ✓. \(5^1\): odd, needs one more \(5\).

steps.stem:
\(a\) and \(b\) are integers.
Given: \(a\cdot b=75\).
Which of the following cannot be the value of \(a-b\)?
explanation: Pairs of factors of \(75\): \(1\cdot75\), \(3\cdot25\), \(5\cdot15\).
Their differences: \(75-1=74\), \(25-3=22\), \(15-5=10\) (or the same numbers with a minus sign, if you swap the order).

steps.stem: \(n\) is a positive integer. The fraction \(\frac{n}{18}\) is in lowest terms (it cannot be reduced), and it is less than \(1\). How many different values can \(n\) have?
explanation: Cannot be reduced: \(n\) shares no prime with \(18=2\cdot3^2\). So \(n\) is not divisible by \(2\) or by \(3\).

steps.stem: Given: \(x>44\). There are exactly \(2\) prime numbers between \(44\) and \(x\) (not including \(x\)). Which of the following cannot be the value of \(x\)?
explanation: Exactly two primes: \(47\) and \(53\) are in, and \(59\) is out. Therefore \(53<x\le59\).
\(54\), \(56\) and \(58\) work. \(x=60\) puts \(59\) inside too: three primes ✗.

steps.stem:
\(x\) and \(y\) are positive integers.
Given: \(6^x\cdot5^y=1080\).
\(x+y=?\)
explanation: Break into primes: \(1080=8\cdot135=8\cdot27\cdot5=2^3\cdot3^3\cdot5\).
\(6^x=2^x\cdot3^x\), therefore \(2^x\cdot3^x\cdot5^y=2^3\cdot3^3\cdot5^1\).
Match the exponents: \(x=3\) and \(y=1\). So \(x+y=4\).

steps.stem: \(a\) and \(b\) are positive integers, and \(a\cdot b\) is divisible by \(14\). Which of the following is necessarily true?
explanation: \(14=2\cdot7\), and \(7\) is prime. A prime that divides a product divides one of the factors. So \(a\) or \(b\) is divisible by \(7\) ✓.
The others are not necessarily true: \(a=2\) and \(b=7\) give \(a\cdot b=14\). Neither number is divisible by \(14\), and \(14\) is not divisible by \(28\).
\(a=7\) and \(b=2\) show that \(a\) does not have to be even.

steps.stem: \(p\) and \(q\) are prime numbers, and \(p<q\). \(p+q\) is also a prime number. Which of the following is necessarily true?
explanation: If \(p\) and \(q\) were both odd, \(p+q\) would be even and bigger than \(2\). It would not be prime.
So one of them is the even prime \(2\). Since \(p<q\), \(p=2\).
Example: \(p=2\), \(q=3\), \(p+q=5\). This rules out choice (1) (\(5\ne13\)), choice (3) (\(2+7>3\)) and choice (4).

steps.stem: Given: \(t>1\), and \(t^2\) is a prime number. Which of the following is necessarily true about \(t\)?
explanation: If \(t\) were an integer greater than \(1\), then \(t^2=t\cdot t\) would break into two factors greater than \(1\). It would not be prime.
So \(t\) is not an integer. Example: \(t=\sqrt2\) gives \(t^2=2\), a prime.
\(t\) does not have to be small: \(t=\sqrt{97}\) gives \(t^2=97\), a prime, and \(\sqrt{97}>9\). So choice 4 is not necessarily true.

steps.stem: \(m\) is a positive integer. \(m\) has exactly three different divisors (including \(1\) and \(m\)). Which of the following is necessarily true about \(\sqrt{m}\)?
explanation: Exactly three divisors means \(m=p^2\) for a prime \(p\). Its divisors are \(1\), \(p\) and \(p^2\).
Then \(\sqrt{m}=\sqrt{p^2}=p\), a prime ✓.
The others are not necessarily true: \(m=9\) gives \(\sqrt{m}=3\), which is odd and not divisible by \(5\). And \(\sqrt{m}=p\) is always an integer.

steps.stem: \(n\) is a positive integer. The number of different positive divisors of \(n\) (including \(1\) and \(n\)) is odd. Which of the following is necessarily true?
explanation: Divisors come in pairs: \(d\) and \(\frac{n}{d}\). The count is odd only if one divisor is its own partner: \(d=\frac{n}{d}\), that is, \(n=d^2\).
So \(n\) is a perfect square, and \(\sqrt{n}\) is an integer.
The others are not necessarily true: \(n=16\) has \(5\) divisors, but \(16\) is not prime, not odd, and \(\sqrt{16}=4\) is even.

steps.stem:
Alan says: "Every number that is divisible by both \(4\) and \(6\) is also divisible by \(24\)."
Beth says: "Every number that is divisible by both \(4\) and \(6\) is also divisible by \(12\)."
Which of the following is correct?
explanation: \(4=2^2\) and \(6=2\cdot3\). The LCM takes every prime at its higher power: \(2^2\cdot3=12\). So every such number divides by \(12\): Beth is right.
Alan is wrong: \(12\) is divisible by \(4\) and by \(6\), but not by \(24\).
\(24\) is just \(4\cdot6\). The product is too big because \(4\) and \(6\) share a factor of \(2\).

steps.stem: \(n\) is an integer, and \(1<n<120\). \(n\) is not divisible by \(2\), \(3\), \(5\) or \(7\). Which of the following is necessarily true?
choices: The last digit of \(n\) is \(1\), \(3\) or \(7\).
explanation: If \(n\) were not prime, it would break into two factors, and the smaller one would be at most \(\sqrt{n}<\sqrt{121}=11\).
Then \(n\) would have a prime factor smaller than \(11\): \(2\), \(3\), \(5\) or \(7\). But none of them divides \(n\). So \(n\) is prime ✓.
The others are not necessarily true: \(n=113\) is not less than \(100\); \(n=19\) ends in \(9\); \(n=11\) is not greater than \(11\).

steps.stem: \(a\), \(b\), \(c\) are different positive integers, and \(x=a\cdot b^2\cdot c^3\). Which of the following cannot be the value of \(x\)?
explanation: One of the numbers may be \(1\).
\(21=3\cdot7\): if \(c\ge2\), then \(c^3\ge8\) must divide \(21\) — impossible. So \(c=1\).
Then \(b\ne1\) (the numbers are different). \(b^2\) must be \(4\), \(9\) or \(16\) (bigger squares are more than \(21\)), and none of them divides \(21\) ✗.
So \(x\) cannot be \(21\).

steps.stem: \(n\) is a positive integer. \(n^2\) has a divisor that is greater than \(2n\) and different from \(n^2\). What is the smallest possible value of \(n\)?
explanation: Check the choices, starting from the smallest.
\(n=4\): the divisors of \(16\) are \(1\), \(2\), \(4\), \(8\), \(16\). Only \(16\) itself is greater than \(8\) ✗.
\(n=5\): the divisors of \(25\) are \(1\), \(5\), \(25\). None fits ✗.
So the smallest \(n\) is \(6\).
